clinicalPearls: A mucous cyst is a ganglion arising from the distal interphalangeal joint and is intimately associated with underlying osteoarthritis of that joint.
It typically presents in older adults as a small, dome-shaped, translucent swelling on the dorsum of the finger between the DIP joint and the nail fold.
Compression of the germinal nail matrix by the cyst commonly produces a longitudinal groove or ridge in the nail plate, a useful diagnostic clue.
An osteophyte at the DIP joint is almost always present and is considered a key driver; addressing it at surgery reduces recurrence.
Progressive attenuation of the overlying skin risks spontaneous rupture and a direct communication to the joint, creating a portal for septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.
Management ranges from observation to surgical excision with osteophyte debridement; excision that includes the joint pedicle and osteophyte offers the most durable results.
When skin over the cyst is thin or ulcerated, a local rotation or advancement flap may be needed to achieve stable soft-tissue cover.
Repeated aspiration or needling is associated with recurrence and carries a risk of introducing infection into the DIP joint, so it is generally discouraged.
reference.pathophysiology: A digital mucous cyst is a ganglion of the distal interphalangeal joint that develops in the setting of osteoarthritis. Marginal osteophytes and degenerative capsular changes are thought to promote herniation of mucin-rich synovial fluid through a capsular defect, forming a mucin-filled pseudocyst connected to the joint by a pedicle. The cyst tracks dorsally between the extensor terminal tendon and the collateral structures towards the nail fold, where pressure on the germinal matrix disturbs nail growth. As with other ganglia the lesion lacks a true epithelial lining and recurs if the underlying joint communication and osteophyte are not addressed.
additionalDifferentials: Heberden node of distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis
Dorsal wrist or digital ganglion arising elsewhere
Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
Gouty tophus at the distal interphalangeal joint
Subungual or periungual tumour deforming the nail
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical from the typical site, translucency and associated nail groove
Plain radiographs of the digit to demonstrate distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis and osteophytes
Ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion and its joint connection when uncertain
MRI reserved for atypical or recurrent lesions
Transillumination of the cyst at the bedside
Assessment of overlying skin integrity to plan soft-tissue cover
Microbiological sampling if there is discharge or suspected secondary infection
redFlags: Skin breakdown or discharge with signs of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the distal interphalangeal joint
Cellulitis or ascending infection of the digit
Rapidly enlarging or atypical solid mass suggesting alternative pathology
Marked nail plate destruction raising concern for a subungual tumour
reference.prognosis: Benign but linked to progressive distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis; surgical excision with osteophyte removal gives good durable results, whereas simple aspiration frequently recurs and the associated arthritis continues to progress.
pitfalls: Repeatedly needling or aspirating the cyst, risking recurrence and inoculation of the DIP joint
Failing to remove the associated osteophyte, the principal cause of recurrence
Not recognising thin or ulcerated overlying skin that requires flap cover rather than simple closure
Overlooking an established communication with the joint that predisposes to septic arthritis
Attributing a nail deformity to a primary nail disorder rather than matrix compression by the cyst
references: British Society for Surgery of the Hand guidance on digital ganglia
management: Observation for small, asymptomatic cysts with intact overlying skin
Surgical excision of the cyst with debridement of the distal interphalangeal osteophyte and ligation of the joint pedicle for a durable cure
Local rotation or advancement flap for soft-tissue cover where the overlying skin is attenuated
Avoid repeated needle aspiration or sclerotherapy, which frequently recur and risk seeding septic arthritis
Symptomatic management of the underlying distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis with analgesia and splinting
Monitor skin integrity and counsel prompt review if the cyst ruptures, given the risk of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis
Refer to hand surgery for excision when there is nail deformity, persistent pain or threatened skin
